Do foods that taste good together also work well together for your body?

We studied shared flavor molecules and nutrient teamwork in food pairs.

Short answerFlavor sharing and nutrient teamwork show almost no link; more flavor sharing goes with slightly less nutrient teamwork.
Real recipe pairs: 0.22; random pairs: 0.26. The chance this is just luck is less than 0.01; this is unlikely to be luck.
Clearer patterns appear in North American, Western European, Southern European, South Asian. We cannot be sure about Latin American, Northern and Eastern European, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern and North African, African.

What is this project?

Some foods share flavor molecules. Cooks often say these foods taste good together.

We asked if those pairs also fill each other's missing nutrients.

Nutrient teamwork means how well two foods fill each other's missing nutrients.

We used the Ahn et al. 2011 flavor database, 57,691 real recipes, and the USDA food database.

Two ideas in one minute

Flavor sharing

How many flavor molecules two foods have in common.

Example: tomato and cheese share some flavor molecules.

Nutrient teamwork

How often one food is low where the other is high.

The score runs from 0 (no help) to 1 (helps a lot). We looked at 11 nutrients.

Example: rice and beans can help cover different nutrient gaps.

How we did it

Pick 219 common foods.
Match each food to USDA nutrition.
Score every pair: 23,871 pairs.
Compare recipe pairs with random pairs.
Repeat the check for 10 world regions.

What we found

Almost No Link

Flavor sharing and nutrient teamwork

Link score: -0.10 (almost no link; more flavor sharing goes with slightly less nutrient teamwork). Without spices and herbs: 0.00 (almost no link; more flavor sharing goes with slightly more nutrient teamwork).

Slightly lower

Real recipes versus random pairs

Real recipe pairs: 0.22; random pairs: 0.26. The chance this is just luck is less than 0.01; this is unlikely to be luck.

Varies by region

Different food regions

Clearer patterns appear in North American, Western European, Southern European, South Asian. We cannot be sure about Latin American, Northern and Eastern European, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern and North African, African.

Charts

Foods that share flavor do not fill more gaps

What you are looking at: Each dot area represents many food pairs.

How to read it: Look for a rising or falling cloud.

What it tells us: The cloud is mostly flat, so the link is small.

Real recipe pairs versus random pairs

What you are looking at: One real-pair score and a gray random range.

How to read it: Compare the blue line with the gray band.

What it tells us: The real pairs score lower in this check.

The pattern differs by region

What you are looking at: Region scores and their likely ranges.

How to read it: Gray means the range includes no link.

What it tells us: Some regions show a clearer pattern than others.

Example pairs

What you are looking at: Scores for our picks and random pairs.

How to read it: Longer bars mean more nutrient teamwork.

What it tells us: Familiar pairs are not always the highest scoring.

Spices and herbs change the picture

What you are looking at: The link score under different nutrient cut-offs.

How to read it: Compare the two colored series.

What it tells us: Removing spice and herb effects matters for interpretation.

Things to keep in mind

  • Numbers use 100 grams of raw food.
  • Recipes have no ingredient amounts.
  • We chose some food matches ourselves. For example, bean means pinto beans, and cheese means cheddar.
  • We left out 33 vague foods, such as fish, meat, and truffle.
  • The flavor data comes from one book.
  • Spices and herbs behave differently. This shows a pattern, not a cause.

Glossary

Flavor molecule
A tiny chemical linked to smell and taste.
Nutrient teamwork
How well two foods fill each other's missing nutrients.
Pair
Two foods studied together.
Link score
A number describing how two measures move together.
Likely range
A range showing uncertainty around a result.
Random comparison
A check against pairs made by chance.
Chance this is luck
How easily random choices could produce the result.
Region
A group of cuisines from a part of the world.
